newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Take profits from rising Europe.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Take profits from rising Europe.

text.p: International investors should be wary of further gains in European bond markets, giddy from a deal on European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and from weak U.S. data, analysts said on Tuesday.
"You don't want to be chasing the rally higher," said Kirit Shah, chief strategist at Sanwa International in London. "All the good news is priced in."

Italian bond futures hit an all-time high of 132.67 and Spanish bond futures set a high of 116.89 on Tuesday, after European Union (EU) leaders said on Monday they had reached an agreement on the EMU budget stability pact and adopted a resolution on growth and employment.
The growth and employment resolution was designed to appease the French domestic electorate, but lacked bite, analysts said.
"EU leaders had to come up with a deal. They would have brought in a charter for peace on earth if necessary," said Shah.

September Bund futures also hit a contract high of 101.88 on Tuesday. Markets are benefiting too from recent weak economic data from the U.S., analysts said. May U.S. consumer price data will be released at 1230 GMT on Tuesday.
"There is a belief that there will be no more rate hikes in the U.S. -- it's nothing to do with positive EMU convergence," said Shah.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese bonds will benefit from yesterday's boost to a timely introduction of EMU, said Teis Knuthsen, director of European analysis at First Chicago.
"We are very bullish for the front end of Southern Europe on a relative basis to Germany, but against a background of rising core bond yields."
Ten-year Spain/Germany bond spreads can narrow to 50 basis points from their current 68 basis points, Knuthsen said.
Philip Tyson, senior international economist at HSBC Markets, also favoured the front end of Spain and Italy.
"We will see flatter, lower peripheral yield curves."
The Italy/German 10-year spread can edge in to 130 basis points by early next year from its current 133, Tyson said.
"But that's after being at 150-160 basis points," he said.
But Spanish bonds had more mileage in them, and could squeeze in to 30 basis points on a 10-year basis against Bunds, Tyson added.
"It seems that EMU will go ahead in the first wave with Spain and not with Italy. That will provide a brief hiccup for BTPs," he said.
Interest rates also need to come down in Spain and Italy to encourage investors to take bond positions, analysts said.
"The cost of carry is fairly high, because of the short-term rates," said Knuthsen.
Analysts hope the Bank of Italy will cut interest rates if preliminary June inflation data from Italian cities, due in the next week, are as low as forecast.
Meanwhile, the Bank of Spain may ease further at its next 10-day repo tender, analysts added.
But European spreads will narrow, Knuthsen said, largely because German and French bond markets will fall.
"German and French bond yields are expensive compared with their business cycles."

In addition, Knuthsen saw as negative Tuesday's comments by French European Affairs Minister Pierre Moscovici that France will make the final decision to join the euro once it assesses the state of public finances.
"There is a risk in the French public finances which has not been priced in yet."
